lessons.title: Carbon, carbon dioxide and limestone

objectives: Describe diamond and graphite and link their uses to their structures.
Describe the preparation, tests and uses of carbon dioxide.
Describe the limestone reactions and the carbon cycle.
reviewNotes: Climate statements are kept general and conservative. Preparation of CO₂ and limewater tests are standard practicals; check the syllabus for C₆₀ and carbon monoxide.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Allotropes of carbon
blocks.md: **Allotropes** are different forms of the same element. In **diamond** each carbon atom is bonded to **four** others in a rigid giant covalent structure: it is **very hard**, has a very high melting point and does not conduct: used in drill tips and jewellery. In **graphite** each carbon is bonded to **three** others in flat **layers** that slide over each other, with free electrons between: it is **soft**, slippery and **conducts electricity**: used in pencils, lubricants and electrodes. **Fullerenes** (e.g. C₆₀) are ball-shaped molecules of carbon.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide
blocks.md: **Preparation**: marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; collect by **downward delivery** because CO₂ is denser than air. **Test**: limewater turns milky: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. It does not burn and puts out flames; it dissolves in water to give a weak acid. **Uses**: fizzy drinks, fire extinguishers, dry ice for cooling, baking powder (2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂).

blocks.title: Limestone
blocks.md: Limestone and marble are **calcium carbonate**. Strong heating gives **quicklime**: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Water turns it into **slaked lime**: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, used to **neutralise acid soil**, in cement, mortar and glass making. The carbonate reacts with acids, which is why acid rain damages limestone buildings.

blocks.caption: The carbon cycle (simplified).
blocks.alt: Boxes for carbon dioxide in air, plants, animals and fossil fuels or wood, with arrows for photosynthesis into plants, feeding from plants to animals, respiration from animals to the air and burning from fuels to the air.

blocks.title: Carbon cycle and the greenhouse effect
blocks.md: Plants take CO₂ from the air in **photosynthesis**; animals get carbon by **feeding**; **respiration**, **burning** and **decay** return CO₂ to the air. Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests add CO₂ faster than it is removed. CO₂ and methane are **greenhouse gases**, and scientists link their increase to global warming.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Graphite conducts but diamond does not, although both are pure carbon.
- CO₂ does not support burning; oxygen does.
- Quicklime (CaO) and slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) are different substances; quicklime reacts violently with water.

blocks.title: Why is graphite a lubricant?
blocks.statement: Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant but diamond is not.
steps: Graphite has layers held together by weak forces, so the layers slide.
Diamond has a rigid 3D network of strong bonds: it cannot slide.
blocks.answer: Graphite layers slide; diamond is rigid.

blocks.title: Which gas?
blocks.statement: A gas from marble chips and acid is passed into limewater, which turns milky. Name the gas and the milky substance.
steps: Marble is calcium carbonate: acid releases carbon dioxide.
The milky substance is calcium carbonate.

blocks.title: Crude oil and fractions
blocks.md: **Crude oil** is a mixture of **hydrocarbons** (compounds of carbon and hydrogen only), formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny sea organisms. It is separated by **fractional distillation** in a tall column, hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Small molecules (low boiling points) leave at the top: **refinery gases** (cooking gas, LPG), **petrol**, **kerosene** (jet fuel), **diesel**, **fuel oil**, and at the bottom **bitumen** (roads). Cameroon refines crude oil at the SONARA refinery in Limbe.

blocks.caption: Fractional distillation of crude oil.
blocks.alt: A tall column with heated crude oil entering near the bottom and fractions leaving at different heights: refinery gases at the top, then petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen at the bottom.

blocks.title: Alkanes
blocks.md: **Alkanes** have the general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀. They are **saturated** (single bonds only) and fairly unreactive, but burn: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O and C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. With too little oxygen they burn **incompletely**, giving poisonous **carbon monoxide** and black soot: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O.

items.text: ethene C₂H₄: a C=C double bond (unsaturated)

blocks.caption: Displayed formulae of ethane and ethene.
blocks.alt: Ethane with a single bond between two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms; ethene with a double bond between two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms.

blocks.title: Alkenes and cracking
blocks.md: **Alkenes** have the formula **CₙH₂ₙ** and a **C=C double bond**: ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆. They are **unsaturated** and more reactive. **Test**: they **decolourise bromine water** (orange to colourless) by addition: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂; with hydrogen (nickel catalyst): C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. **Cracking** breaks long alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes by heat and a catalyst: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Alkanes do **not** decolourise bromine water in the dark; alkenes do.
- Count the carbon atoms to find the formula: 5 carbons in an alkane gives C₅H₁₂ (2 × 5 + 2).
- Incomplete combustion makes carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and colourless.

blocks.title: Formula of an alkane

blocks.statement: Bromine water is shaken separately with ethane and ethene. What is seen and what does it show?

Ethene has a C=C double bond: it is unsaturated.

blocks.title: Alcohols and fermentation
blocks.md: **Alcohols** contain the **–OH** group: methanol CH₃OH, **ethanol C₂H₅OH**, propanol C₃H₇OH. Ethanol is made by **fermentation**: yeast acting on sugar **without oxygen** at about 25–35 °C: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Palm wine, raffia wine and corn beer are made this way. The alcohol is made stronger by **fractional distillation**. Ethanol is also made from ethene and steam in industry. It burns: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

blocks.caption: Fermentation of sugar: carbon dioxide is given off.
blocks.alt: A flask of sugar solution and yeast with a delivery tube bubbling gas into a test tube of limewater, which turns milky.

blocks.title: Uses and health
blocks.md: Ethanol is a **solvent** (perfumes, medicines), a **fuel** (alone or mixed with petrol), an **antiseptic** and the alcohol in drinks. **Alcohol is a drug**: it harms the liver and brain, is dangerous when driving, and is not for children or pregnant women. **Methanol** is poisonous and can cause blindness or death if drunk. Home-made spirits can contain it.

blocks.title: Ethanoic acid and esters
blocks.md: Oxidation of ethanol (for example when wine goes sour) gives **ethanoic acid** CH₃COOH, the acid in **vinegar**: a **weak acid**. An **ester** is made from an alcohol and an acid: C₂H₅OH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (ethyl ethanoate). Esters smell sweet and fruity and are used in perfumes and flavourings.

blocks.caption: Making poly(ethene).
blocks.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: many ethene molecules, addition polymerisation, poly(ethene) long chain.

blocks.title: Polymers
blocks.md: A **polymer** is a long molecule made from many small **monomers**. In **addition polymerisation** alkene monomers with C=C bonds join without anything being lost: ethene gives **poly(ethene)** (bags, bottles), propene gives poly(propene), chloroethene gives PVC (pipes). **Natural polymers**: starch, proteins, cellulose. **Plastic waste** does not rot (not biodegradable): it blocks drains, harms animals and pollutes rivers and the sea: reduce, reuse and recycle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Fermentation needs **no oxygen**; with oxygen, vinegar can form instead.
- Monomers are small molecules; the polymer is the long chain.
- Burning plastic gives toxic fumes: never burn plastic waste in the open.

objectives: Describe how soap is made and how it cleans.

reviewNotes: NPK numbers (20-10-10) and the 'kg of N' calculations are illustrative; check local fertiliser products. Soap making with caustic soda is a teacher-led activity and handling advice is general. Industrial ammonia (Haber process) is mentioned only; conditions are covered in Form 5.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Making soap
blocks.md: Soap is made by boiling a **fat or oil** (palm oil, palm kernel oil, groundnut oil) with a strong alkali such as **sodium hydroxide** (caustic soda) or **potassium hydroxide** (potash made from plant ash): **fat or oil + alkali → soap + glycerol**. This reaction is called **saponification**. Salt is added to make the soap separate and float. Caustic soda is **corrosive**: wear eye protection and gloves; keep children away.

items.text: soap lifts grease into the water

blocks.caption: How soap removes grease.
blocks.alt: Grease in the centre surrounded by soap ions whose tails point into the grease and whose heads point out into the water, with a key to the soap ion.

blocks.title: How soap and detergents clean
blocks.md: A soap ion has an **ionic head** that is attracted to **water** and a long **hydrocarbon tail** that is attracted to **grease**. The tails dissolve in the grease and the heads stay in the water, so the grease breaks into tiny droplets that float away. In **hard water** soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions and forms **scum**, using up soap. **Detergents** (soapless detergents, made from petroleum chemicals) do **not** form scum in hard water.

blocks.title: Fertilisers
blocks.md: Plants need **nitrogen (N)** for leaves and growth, **phosphorus (P)** for roots and **potassium (K)** for flowers and fruit: a fertiliser labelled **NPK** contains all three. Common ones: **ammonium nitrate** NH₄NO₃, **urea** CO(NH₂)₂, **ammonium sulphate** (NH₄)₂SO₄, superphosphate, potassium chloride. Ammonia is made industrially from nitrogen and hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, then NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.

blocks.caption: Percentage of nitrogen by mass in three fertilisers.
blocks.alt: A bar chart: urea 46.7, ammonium nitrate 35.0, ammonium sulphate 21.2 percent nitrogen.

blocks.title: Using fertilisers wisely
blocks.md: Too much fertiliser washed into rivers makes algae grow too fast; when they die, bacteria use up the oxygen and fish die (**eutrophication**). Nitrate can also pollute well water. Use the amount recommended, apply before rain with care, and consider organic manure and crop rotation. Farmers should follow the advice of the local agricultural officer.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Soap does not clean by dissolving grease like a solvent: it surrounds droplets with its ions.
- A higher percentage of nitrogen does not mean more is always better: too much harms crops and rivers.
- Detergents are not soap: they are made from different chemicals.

blocks.title: Percentage of nitrogen

blocks.title: Which fertiliser gives more N?
blocks.statement: Which of urea (46.7 % N) or ammonium sulphate (21.2 % N) supplies more nitrogen per 50 kg bag, and how much?
steps: Urea: 0.467 × 50 = 23.35 kg N. Ammonium sulphate: 0.212 × 50 = 10.6 kg N.
